item.title: Wedding celebration planned for December or January, but Barsha dies beforehand
item.description:
Jumratun Nessa Barsha, 24, had been in a relationship with Nabid Hossain, but her parents had objected to it. However, as their daughter was very serious about the relationship, they eventually arranged her marriage to Nabid through a private 'kabin' ceremony on 7 October 2025.

During the year they lived together as husband and wife, Barsha was allegedly subjected to abuse by Nabid several times. He also repeatedly took money from her parents, citing business needs. Even so, Barsha kept returning to him. Their formal wedding celebrations was supposed to take place in December or January. But Barsha died before that could happen.

Members of Barsha’s family said Nabid was beating her even around midnight last Tuesday. Unable to endure the abuse, Barsha made a video call to her father, Sheikh Monowar Hossain, at around 12 midnight and screamed, “Father, come and save me.” Her parents reached her in-laws’ home within 15 to 20 minutes. But when they arrived, Nabid’s family told them that Barsha had “committed suicide”. Later, when her body was taken to Shaheed Suhrawardy Medical College Hospital in the capital, doctors declared her dead.

Barsha’s family refuses to accept the incident as a suicide. Her mother, Hasina Akter, told Prothom Alo today, Thursday, “This cannot be suicide. If my daughter had wanted to kill herself, she would not have called us. In her last video call, she was screaming, ‘Father, come and save me.’”

Barsha’s father, Sheikh Monowar Hossain, filed a murder case with Tejgaon Police Station over the incident. On the night of the incident, Barsha’s family handed Nabid over to the police at Suhrawardy Medical College Hospital.

Speaking to Prothom Alo, Tejgaon Police Station Officer-in-Charge (OC) Muniruzzaman said Nabid Hossain had beaten Barsha at various times over demands for dowry. Marks of injuries were found on her body. Her father filed a case in connection with the incident, and Nabid was subsequently arrested at the hospital.

Woman video-calls father late at night to report abuse, call drops; family finds her dead

Studies stopped before marriage, abuse followed

Sheikh Monowar Hossain and Hasina Akter have three daughters. Barsha was the second. After completing her higher secondary education, she enrolled in the first year of her undergraduate programme at Tejgaon College in Dhaka for the 2024–25 academic year. She met Nabid Hossain while studying at the college, and they developed a romantic relationship. Barsha later told her parents about the relationship.

Barsha’s mother, Hasina Akter, said, “We did not want Barsha to marry Nabid. We tried to make her understand that he was not a good person. But our daughter was determined to marry him. Eventually, the two families were present when they got married in a private ceremony. A few days before the marriage, Nabid stopped my daughter from studying. He did not want her to continue her education.”

Hasina Akter said Nabid’s mother was also keen to have Barsha as her daughter-in-law. She said, “Nabid’s mother, Nurun Nahar, would call every other day and say, ‘Get the kabin done. The boy and girl are going around together, and that is not good. If something happens, we will not be able to show our faces. Get the kabin done now; hold the ceremony later.’ That is why, on 7 October 2025, a kazi was brought in and the marriage was solemnised privately in the presence of Nabid’s parents and us. The formal ceremony was never held afterwards. We were supposed to arrange a celebration this December or January and give the groom a ring, furniture and other things.”

Nabid had previously ‘split Barsha’s head open’

Nabid Hossain allegedly abused Barsha frequently. Speaking to family members, it was learnt that Nabid had once beaten Barsha so badly that he split her head open, six or seven months ago. Barsha’s mother, Hasina Akter, said, “At that time, we took Barsha to Suhrawardy Medical College Hospital and had her head stitched. The hospital also collected information from the police. But after we brought her home from the hospital, Barsha told her father, ‘Leave it, Father. Don’t say anything to him.’ My daughter would not let us take any action against Nabid. So we did not pursue a case or any legal action.”

The family alleges that Nabid also assaulted Barsha on several other occasions. Her mother, Hasina Akter, said Nabid was suspicious of Barsha and did not want her to talk to anyone. Barsha would often call her father and say, “Father, come and take me away. I will not stay here any longer.” But within two days, if Nabid called her, she would return to him.

Barsha’s mother said, “My daughter did not tell us everything. Whenever we noticed something, we would explain to her that this was no way to live and that people could marry twice. We told her to leave him. But she would say Nabid would change for the better, that they were doing fine and so on. We cannot say what was going on in her mind. Even if we brought her home and kept her there, she would run back to him. My daughter was madly in love with him.”

Money demands began soon after the marriage

Barsha’s father, Sheikh Monowar Hossain, is involved in the business of buying and selling land. The family lives in Lalbagh, where they also own two flats which they rent out. Relatives said Nabid Hossain began asking Barsha’s father for money, citing business needs, just a few days after marrying her.

Barsha’s mother, Hasina, said, “Nabid started asking for money a few days after the marriage. He would tell Barsha, ‘I will start a business. Ask your father to give me Tk 100,000.’ My husband’s income is no longer what it used to be because of his illness. Even so, Nabid took money from him many times in this way. My daughter was very close to her father. He would give her whatever she asked for. I would often get angry about it. That is why she did not tell me about these matters.”

Barsha’s mother said Nabid’s parents were also financially well-off. Nabid would take money from them as well. Hasina Akter said, “Perhaps he has some bad habits. The way Nabid beat my daughter, I do not think it would have been possible unless he was addicted to something. Nabid would also quarrel with his own parents. So they could not do anything to him either. Whenever Barsha returned to our home in anger after being beaten, her mother-in-law would say, ‘Send Barsha back. The risk is ours.’”

Prothom Alo tried to contact Nabid Hossain’s father, Manjur Hossain, and mother, Nurun Nahar, by mobile phone to learn their response to the allegations made by Barsha’s family. They did not answer despite repeated calls. The reporter later sent them text messages identifying himself. They then switched off their mobile phones.

item.title: LPG prices rise in markets as commission moves to raise rates again
item.description:
Consumers are having to pay Tk 500 to Tk 700 more than the fixed price for a 12-kg liquefied petroleum gas (LPG) cylinder. Without taking steps to stop sales at inflated prices, the Bangladesh Energy Regulatory Commission (BERC) has moved to increase the commissions of importers and sellers. This could further raise the cost of cooking gas for consumers.

BERC held a daylong public hearing on Thursday on a proposal to increase LPG prices. Importers, distributors and retailers called for higher commissions at the hearing. After evaluating their proposals, a technical committee of the commission recommended an increase of Tk 139 for a 12-kg cylinder. If implemented, the price of a cylinder currently set at Tk 1,837 would rise to Tk 1,976.

Although the commission has 60 days to announce its decision after the hearing, it has asked stakeholders to submit their comments by next Sunday. This leaves only one working day to provide feedback after the hearing. Earlier, BERC announced the hearing on 14 October amid threats of strikes by distributors and retailers. The Consumers Association of Bangladesh (CAB) has alleged that, instead of taking action against sales at inflated prices, the commission is rushing to raise prices.

Companies currently receive Tk 200 per 12-kg cylinder as the cost or commission for storage and bottling. Omera has proposed raising this commission to Tk 478, Petromax to Tk 349 and Delta to Tk 360. Meghna Group has proposed setting it at Tk 300.

Prices may also rise in November as part of the regular monthly adjustment. BERC and importer sources say that, due to increases in global LPG prices and shipping costs, the price of a 12-kg cylinder could rise by more than Tk 100 through the regular adjustment alone. If higher commissions are added, the burden on consumers will increase further.

However, BERC Chairman Jalal Ahmed said a decision would be made after analysing the views expressed by all participants at the hearing. He said complaints that LPG was not being sold at the fixed price were frequently raised, although it had also sometimes been sold at lower prices. As the costs, including commissions, were set in 2021, they could now be revised.

The LPG market has remained volatile for one and a half months. Prices were raised once in early October. Even after that, sales at higher prices have continued. Of the 35 companies involved in the LPG business in the country, 23 have import infrastructure, but only 10 imported LPG last month.

Legal action if strikes called to destabilise LPG market: Energy minister

Companies currently receive Tk 200 per 12-kg cylinder as the cost or commission for storage and bottling. Omera has proposed raising this commission to Tk 478, Petromax to Tk 349 and Delta to Tk 360. Meghna Group has proposed setting it at Tk 300.

Meanwhile, distributors have sought to raise their commission from Tk 50 to Tk 150, while retailers have applied for an increase from Tk 45 to Tk 70. A proposal has also been made to raise the commission on autogas used in vehicles from Tk 8 to Tk 11 per litre.

The private sector controls 99 per cent of the LPG market. Of the total LPG consumed, 80 per cent is used for cooking. More than 10 million customers use LPG. Although BERC has been adjusting prices every month since April 2021, consumers often have to pay more than the fixed rates.

Distributors have sought to raise their commission from Tk 50 to Tk 150, while retailers have applied for an increase from Tk 45 to Tk 70. A proposal has also been made to raise the commission on autogas used in vehicles from Tk 8 to Tk 11 per litre.

‘The market will not stabilise unless prices are raised’

After analysing the proposals, a technical committee formed by BERC said the price of a 12-kg cylinder could be set at Tk 1,976, with an increase of Tk 139. As part of this increase, the committee proposed raising the distributor-level commission from Tk 50 to Tk 80 and the retailer-level commission from Tk 45 to Tk 70.

Business representatives said the market would not stabilise unless prices were set at reasonable levels. They said this was not a demand raised suddenly; they had been making it to BERC for two years. A proposal to increase prices had been submitted a year ago. BERC had now arranged the hearing under pressure from the market situation. The commission for importers would have to be increased by Tk 100, distributors’ commission to Tk 70 and retailers’ commission to Tk 105. This would mean an increase of Tk 275. If this were implemented, no one would sell LPG at higher prices.

Abu Sayed Raza, chief marketing officer of Meghna Fresh LPG, said prices should be set after taking all factors into account so that no one could charge even one taka more than the fixed rate in the market. Prices must therefore be reasonable. The government could then take strict action against any deviation in the market.

The LPG market has remained volatile for one and a half months. Prices were raised once in early October. Even after that, sales at higher prices have continued. Of the 35 companies involved in the LPG business, 23 have import infrastructure, but only 10 imported LPG last month.

Mani Mukta Pal, proprietor of Messrs Ujjal Traders, speaking on behalf of distributors, said their costs had also increased, just as operators had reported rising costs. At the same time, distributors had to bear the burden of idle cylinders. She demanded that distributors’ commission be set at Tk 150 per cylinder.

Serajul Mawla, president of the LPG Autogas owners Association, said more than 200,000 vehicles run on LPG. A commission of Tk 8 per litre had been set in 2021, and five years have passed since then. Operating costs have increased. Some stations in cities were making profits, but 80 per cent were operating at a loss. He demanded that the commission be set at Tk 11.

Speaking at the hearing on behalf of companies unable to import due to letter of credit (LC) complications, Anup Kumar Sen, chief operating officer of Orion Gas Limited, said 10 companies were unable to import under the new circumstances. Their infrastructure was lying unused, creating a shortage of cylinders in the market. It was not possible to buy LPG from other companies and sell it at the price set by BERC.

Consumers Oppose Price Hike

LPG importers and BERC faced strong criticism at the public hearing on the proposed price increase. Consumers raised widespread questions about the failure to ensure sales at government-fixed prices and the regulator’s inaction. Some distributors and retailers also questioned the importers.

Abu Taher Qureshi, speaking on behalf of distributors, said bottled LPG was supposed to be delivered to distributors’ premises. But whenever a shortage began, suppliers stopped deliveries. This added to costs and made it impossible to sell at the fixed price.

Syed Mizanur Rahman, who attended the hearing as a representative of the Bangladesh Economic Association, said the association was boycotting the hearing in protest against LPG being sold at prices higher than those fixed by BERC, the collection of additional charges and the failure to take action over these complaints.

Abu Sayed Raza, chief marketing officer of Meghna Fresh LPG, said prices should be set after taking all factors into account so that no one could charge even one taka more than the fixed rate in the market. Prices must therefore be reasonable. The government could then take strict action against any deviation in the market.
LPG 12kg cylinder price rises by Tk 252

Khalilur Rahman, a representative of CAB, presented seven written demands on behalf of the organisation. He said it was BERC’s responsibility to look after consumers’ interests. Without doing so, the hearing would not be meaningful. He called for no increase in prices and demanded that sales and purchases at the rates announced by BERC be ensured.

The importing companies said BERC sets new prices every month based on Saudi Aramco contract prices, premiums (shipping and insurance costs), the dollar exchange rate and fuel prices. However, other costs had also increased over the past five years. Prices therefore needed to be revised.

M Shamsul Alam, CAB’s energy adviser, told Prothom Alo that companies have proposed another price increase while selling LPG in the market at whatever prices they chose. No action has been taken against sales at inflated prices. By rushing to raise prices, the commission was essentially going through the motions. The prices has, in effect, already been decided. This had failed to ensure energy justice for consumers.

item.title: Ex-Air Force officer Tahsif’s death: Friend Dwip taken into police custody
item.description:
Police have taken Dwip, a younger friend of former Air Force officer KM Tahsif Souri, 28, into custody in connection with Tahsif’s death. The Police Bureau of Investigation (PBI) took him into custody.

Dwip was taken from a house in the capital’s Mohammadpur area late on Thursday night. Md Abu Yusuf, superintendent of police, for PBI’s Law and Media wing, confirmed the information on Friday morning.

Ex-Air Force officer’s body recovered from Turag River

Abu Yusuf said Dwip had been taken to the PBI Metro North office in connection with Tahsif’s death. As the two had gone out and were together on the night before the incident, Dwip would be questioned about it, he said. The information he provided would be checked and verified.

Tahsif left his home in Uttara, in the capital, on Tuesday evening. At 1.35 am that night, he sent his mother a voice message on her mobile phone saying he was on his way home. However, he never returned.

Police recovered his body from the Turag River on Wednesday afternoon. His relatives said the motorcycle he had taken with him when he left home was also missing.

Ex-Air Force officer Tahsif identified through mobile phone found with body

Before Tahsif went missing, CCTV footage showed him with a man. Family members identified the man as Dwip.

The footage shows Tahsif meeting the man in front of a garage at the Rajuk Uttara Apartment Project in Sector 18 of Uttara on Tuesday night. After shaking hands, the two left on separate motorcycles.

Tahsif’s father, KM Eneyetul Karim, told Prothom Alo that in the evening on the day of the incident, Dwip, a younger friend of Tahsif’s, came downstairs to call him. Tahsif went down, saying he would speak to Dwip and return. He never came back home.

Ex-Air Force officer’s body recovered: Home minister declines to comment for now

CCTV footage from the building later showed Tahsif and Dwip leaving on separate motorcycles at 6.31 pm on Tuesday, said his father.

Police officials said an investigation was needed to establish Dwip’s role in Tahsif’s disappearance and the subsequent recovery of his body.

Tahsif’s body underwent a post-mortem examination at the morgue of Shaheed Suhrawardy Medical College on Thursday. It was later handed over to his family. He was buried in Uttara on Thursday after funeral prayers.

Tahsif’s father, KM Eneyetul Karim, has expressed suspicion over his son’s death. He said it was not suicide and that the government would be able to identify those responsible if it investigated the matter.

item.title: 'Star Trek', 'X-Men' star Patrick Stewart dead at 86
item.description:
PEOPLE-PATRICK STEWART/

Patrick Stewart, the British Shakespearean actor who became a Hollywood megastar through roles in the "Star Trek" and "X-Men" franchises, has died at his home in Los Angeles. He was 86.

His death on Wednesday came after a "brief and poignant journey" with Alzheimer's disease and Lewy body dementia, according to an official statement on his social media accounts.

"His sonorous voice and singular talent will forever be synonymous with indelible performances in every genre," the statement said.

The actor, who hailed from the northern English region of Yorkshire, trod the boards in Britain with the Royal Shakespeare Company and the National Theatre in London, and worked on British television.

But he rocketed into the pop culture history books in his mid-40s when he was cast as Captain Jean-Luc Picard in "Star Trek: The Next Generation," and then again as Professor Charles Xavier in multiple "X-Men" and related Marvel films.

'Breaking Bad' actor RJ Mitte dead: representatives

A proud Yorkshireman, Stewart "wore his heart on his sleeve, which made him a man to rely on, to admire and in my case, love," Ian McKellan said of his "X-Men" co-star and dear friend.

McKellan, 87, recounted meeting Stewart in London and hearing about his "Star Trek" offer, warning him he may get lost in Hollywood and to think of his stage career.

"Well, he took the risk and thank goodness for us all that he did."

Aboard the Enterprise

Stewart was 47 when he debuted as Picard in "Star Trek: The Next Generation," the first live-action television spinoff of the trailblazing late-1960s sci-fi series.

He effectively filled the boots of William Shatner's Captain Kirk -- to resounding success, both in the TV series and in several films.

Picard became known for a few catchphrases including "Make it so" and "Engage!"

But his move to America in 1987 was initially greeted with disdain by the Los Angeles Times, who wrote him off as an "unknown British Shakespearean actor."

Stewart later dubbed suggestions he was "slumming it" by moving into US television offensive.

He once called his Shakespearean bona fides "nothing but a preparation for sitting in the captain's chair of the Enterprise."

'Colossus of both stage and screen'

Stewart found further acclaim in the "X-Men" series, debuting in 2000 as Professor Charles Xavier, the founder and mentor of the mutant superhero team.

"For more than 25 years, he brought a gravitas and profundity to the role, earning fans across the globe," Marvel Studios said Thursday.

Longtime co-star Hugh Jackman, who played Wolverine, remembered Stewart as both "one of the greats of stage and screen" and "a tremendous friend and man."

Stewart is to make his final on-screen film appearance as Professor Xavier in "Avengers: Doomsday," set for release in December.

"What a heartbreaking week it has been," posted Shatner.

Stewart's death marked the second in days from the "Star Trek" universe, following that of Walter Koenig, who played Chekov in the original series.

Nana Patekar dies after cardiac arrest at residence

Shatner said Stewart -- who most recently played Picard in 2023 -- brought "intelligence, grace and a deep sense of humanity to everything he did."

Stewart earned four Emmy nominations but never won. He did nab a spoken word Grammy, for his narration of "Prokofiev: Peter And The Wolf."

And even as he found success in Hollywood, Stewart's love of theater, and the bard in particular, never left him.

Between filming, he would return to the stage, winning two Olivier awards.

Shakespeare, Stewart said, "feels like a friend, someone who just went out of the room to get another bottle of wine."

The Royal Shakespeare Company called him "a colossus of both stage and screen and one of the finest classical Shakespearean actors of his generation."

Troubled start

Stewart was born on 13 July, 1940 in the small West Yorkshire town of Mirfield, the third of three brothers in a working-class family.

His father, back from World War II and perhaps suffering from PTSD, would often beat Stewart's mother -- which prompted Stewart to later work with the charity Refuge, which specializes in domestic abuse.

The actor left school at 15, and studied at Bristol Old Vic Drama School beginning in 1957, making his professional acting debut two years later.

Prematurely balding, Stewart missed out on many of the young romantic leads but quickly slotted into theater life, joining the RSC in 1966 and staying there until 1982.

Any misgivings Stewart had about taking the Picard role in the "Star Trek" universe were mollified by the thought it would be a one-season failure.

He was wrong.

"It changed my life," he said.

Knighted in 2010, Stewart married three times: to Sheila Falconer, with whom he had two children; briefly to "Star Trek" producer Wendy Neuss; and most recently to American singer Sunny Ozell, 38 years his junior.

item.title: Russia's blockade of Ukraine is a threat to global food security — and Bangladesh should take note
item.description:
At a time when 7.8 per cent of the world’s population faces hunger, one of the world’s most important grain routes is again under attack. Russia is choking off Ukraine’s ability to export food through the Black Sea, the Danube River and overland corridors. Its deliberate strikes on ports, warehouses, inland logistics, shipping and agricultural infrastructure are an assault on global food security, disrupting trade, energy and fertiliser markets.

This is a hard economic and humanitarian fact: when grain cannot leave Ukraine, global markets tighten, prices rise and vulnerable countries pay the price.

The timing could hardly be worse. As Ukraine entered the harvest season in August, attacks on transport routes and export facilities trapped grain, oilseeds and other agricultural products inside the country. Grain exports in August were cut by half compared with 2025. International prices have already reacted. And the pressure may intensify in the months ahead.

In October, Ukraine risks running out of storage capacity. By November, more than 9 million tonnes of grain, oilseeds and meal could remain outside available storage. A harvest capable of feeding millions could instead be left stranded. If farmers are unable to sell this season’s crop, they will have less cash for the next sowing season, reducing future production and compounding the crisis into next year.

That matters in a world where an estimated 645 million people already face hunger. Disruptions to maritime routes, energy markets, trade flows and humanitarian logistics do reverberate far beyond the immediate conflict zone as the concurrent crisis in the Middle East demonstrates. The most exposed countries and communities are the least able to absorb another shock to food prices and supplies.

Bangladesh is one of the countries that should be watching particularly closely. Wheat is this country’s second-most-consumed cereal, and Bangladesh relies on imports for more than 80 per cent of its wheat-based food needs.

That dependence leaves Bangladesh exposed to disruptions in major wheat-producing regions and to instability along global trade routes. It is not a theoretical risk. When the war disrupted supply starting four years ago, Bangladesh felt the consequences quickly through higher import costs and rising domestic prices for wheat and wheat-based foods.  Inflation has remained high. 

Russia has understood this from the start. Weaponising food insecurity has been part of its broader strategy since the beginning of its full-scale war of aggression. By targeting Ukraine’s export routes, Russia is not only trying to weaken Kyiv. It is also testing how much pressure the rest of the world will tolerate when food becomes collateral damage. Bangladesh is part of the collateral damage.

Ukraine’s role in world food markets explains why this matters so much. Before February 2022, Ukraine supplied 15 per cent of global corn exports, 10 per cent of wheat exports, 15 to 20 per cent of barley exports and fully 50 per cent of sunflower oil exports. It has long extended its agricultural reach deep into Asian markets. A strong harvest is again expected this year. But harvests only contribute to food security if they can reach the ports, the ships and, ultimately, the people who need them.

International efforts to ease the pressure have become a critical alternative route for Ukrainian exports and a lifeline for Ukraine’s economy.

 But while overland and river alternatives can mitigate the damage, they cannot substitute for safe maritime navigation on the scale global food markets require. Indeed, freedom of maritime navigation is a global security concern, including to Bangladesh.

Open and predictable international food trade is not an abstract concern but an issue on which responsible partners need to take a stand. That is why we call for an urgent moratorium on attacks against grain export facilities, infrastructure and civilian shipping in the Black Sea. It would protect critical infrastructure, restore some stability to food markets and give farmers, traders and import-dependent governments the predictability they need.

The world must not allow food to become yet another weapon of war. A ceasefire leading to a just and lasting peace is necessary to end the daily suffering of Ukrainians and to stabilise a global food system on which millions depend. If Russia ends its war and stops attacking Ukraine’s trade lifelines, the benefits will be felt far beyond Europe — including in Bangladesh, where food security depends not only on what is grown at home, but on what can safely move across the sea.

item.title: Eating fruit has become a luxury in Bangladesh
item.description:
Fruit prices in Bangladesh have risen year after year, putting them beyond the reach of low-income people.

Oranges are in high demand as part of the diet recommended for dengue patients. In July 2020, a kilogram of oranges cost Tk 120–150 in markets in the capital. The same oranges now sell for Tk 350–380 per kg. Prices were even higher on September, reaching Tk 420–450 per kg.

A report by the Bangladesh Trade and Tariff Commission (BTTC), an agency under the Ministry of Commerce, says the government has increased duties and taxes on oranges, apples, pears and grapes year after year. As a result, government revenue has risen, but these fruits have become unaffordable for many people.

Market analysts say that while imported fruits have become more expensive, locally grown fruits have not remained cheap either. Prices of domestic fruits have also increased.

For example, four bananas cost Tk 20–25 in July 2020, compared with Tk 40–50 now. Smaller bananas are available at slightly lower prices. However, buying a single banana from a tea stall costs Tk 15.

On 21 September, Prothom Alo published a report on fruit prices under the headline “Why does an orange now cost Tk 100 and a green coconut Tk 150–220?”

Following its publication, the Ministry of Commerce held a meeting with fruit traders on 3 October. The ministry then instructed the Tariff Commission to prepare a report with recommendations on the tax burden and prices of fruit.

The commission submitted its report to the Ministry of Commerce on Tuesday. According to the report obtained from ministry sources, an examination of the duty and tax structure for fresh fruit imports shows that Bangladesh classifies fresh fruit as a luxury item. In other words, eating fruit has now become a luxury.

Why does an orange now cost Tk 100 and a green coconut Tk 150–220?

Asked whether the government plans to reduce duties and taxes on fruit, Commerce Minister Khandaker Abdul Muktadir told Prothom Alo on Wednesday evening, “Work is under way at the government level on this issue (reducing taxes on fruit). I cannot say anything more for the time being.”

Why eating fruit is essential

Fish, meat, milk, eggs and fruit are essential for meeting the body's nutritional needs. Generally, as people's per capita income rises, they consume fewer carbohydrate-rich foods, such as rice, and eat more fish, meat, milk, eggs and fruit.

According to the Bangladesh Bureau of Statistics' (BBS) Household Income and Expenditure Survey 2010, the average daily fruit consumption per person in the country stood at 45 grams at the time.

The 2016 survey recorded a decline to 36 grams. The 2022 survey showed that fruit consumption had risen to 95.4 grams, although questions remain about the BBS survey findings.

The latest picture of fruit consumption remains unclear because the BBS has not conducted another Household Income and Expenditure Survey since 2022. However, many believe that rising prices have reduced fruit consumption.

Professor SK Roy, a nutritionist and chairperson of the Bangladesh Breastfeeding Foundation, told Prothom Alo, “Low-income people are eating less fish, meat and eggs, which means they are not meeting their vitamin and mineral requirements. International standards recommend that a person consume 400 grams of fruit a day. However, people in Bangladesh get to eat far less fruit than that.”

Government revenue rises as fruit becomes unaffordable

The Tariff Commission’s report shows that the total tax burden on apples, oranges, grapes, pears, pomegranates and other fruits stood at 89 per cent in the 2020–21 fiscal year, including import duty, supplementary duty, regulatory duty and value-added tax (VAT).

In other words, the government collected Tk 89 in duties and taxes on fruit worth Tk 100. The rate has since risen steadily, reaching 122 per cent in the current 2026–27 fiscal year. This means the government collects Tk 122 in duties and taxes on fruit worth Tk 100.

Bangladesh imposes a higher tax burden on fruit than neighbouring countries. The combined duties and taxes on apples and pears range from 60 to 61 per cent in India, 60 to 80 per cent in Pakistan, 25 to 35 per cent in Nepal and 50 to 60 per cent in Sri Lanka.

A report presented at a meeting at the Ministry of Commerce on 3 October stated that apples, oranges, tangerines and grapes were more expensive in Bangladesh than in India, Pakistan and Nepal. At the time, apples cost Tk 150–220 per kg in India, Tk 110–170 in Pakistan and Tk 160–240 in Nepal. In Bangladesh, the price ranged from Tk 380 to Tk 480 per kg.

The Tariff Commission’s report also shows that the government earned Tk 25.70 billion in revenue from fruit in the 2020–21 fiscal year. This figure rose to Tk 59.38 billion in the latest fiscal year, 2025–26.

Although government revenue has increased, fruit imports have declined. Bangladesh imported 800,000 tonnes of fruit in the 2020–21 fiscal year. By 2025–26, the volume had fallen to 571,000 tonnes.

Despite lower imports, the government’s revenue increased as higher prices raised the tax receipts. Meanwhile, the rising value of the US dollar, alongside duties and taxes, has also pushed up fruit prices.

Market analysts believe that declining imports of foreign fruit reduce competition, allowing domestic fruit sellers to charge higher prices as well.

Meanwhile, some people can eat only certain fruits because of physical conditions. For example, economist and former Bangladesh Bank Governor Ahsan H Mansur told Prothom Alo on September that he could not eat any fruit other than apples and pears. His physician had advised him against eating other fruits.

Children sometimes refuse to eat fruits other than a few specific varieties. Wahidur Rahman, a resident of Mirpur in Dhaka, faces this problem.

The private-sector employee told Prothom Alo, “My six-year-old son likes apples. He often says, ‘Dad, bring me some apples.’ I cannot tell him that apples cost Tk 400 per kg and that I cannot afford to buy them.”

He added that three guavas weigh about one kilogram and cost Tk 120, meaning each guava costs Tk 40. “So, can we really say that locally grown fruits are cheap?” he asked.

Recommendation to reduce duties and taxes

The Tariff Commission has recommended reducing duties and taxes on fruit. The commission said Bangladesh does not have sufficient commercial production of apples, oranges, grapes, pears and pomegranates.

As a result, the country depends entirely on imports of these fruits, and the existing tax structure does not protect any domestic horticultural industry by promoting competition.

The commission noted that imposing high duties and taxes on fruit as though it were a luxury item does not support a protective tariff policy. Instead, it causes abnormal price increases in the domestic market, putting nutrient-rich food beyond the reach of ordinary and low-income people. This also discourages legal imports.

Selim Raihan, professor of economics at the University of Dhaka and executive director of the South Asian Network on Economic Modeling (SANEM), told Prothom Alo, “There is no justification for treating fruit as a luxury item. The government increased duties and taxes because of the dollar crisis. That crisis no longer exists. Therefore, duties and taxes on fruit can be reduced.”

item.title: PM returns home after four-day Japan visit
item.description:
Prime Minister Tarique Rahman returned home early today wrapping up his four-day official visit to Japan aimed at strengthening bilateral ties, attracting investment and expanding trade and economic cooperation between the two countries.

“A Biman Bangladesh Airlines flight carrying the Prime Minister, his wife Dr Zubaida Rahman and members of his entourage landed at Hazrat Shahjalal International Airport in Dhaka at 2:48 am,” said Prime Minister’s Deputy Press Secretary Shahadat Shadhin.

Earlier, the flight departed Narita International Airport in Tokyo at 10:55pm local time on 29 October, he added.

At the invitation of Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi, Tarique Rahman’s visit featured high-level bilateral talks, the signing of cooperation agreements, discussions with Japanese business leaders on investment opportunities in Bangladesh, and visits to major industrial and energy facilities.

During the bilateral summit at the Japanese Prime Minister’s Office on 27 October, Tarique Rahman and Takaichi discussed strengthening the longstanding partnership between the two countries, with particular emphasis on trade, investment, energy security, infrastructure, technology, space research and regional and international affairs.

The two leaders also discussed a proposed private investment of one trillion Japanese yen (US$6.3 billion) in Bangladesh’s energy, infrastructure and information and communication technology (ICT) sectors.

They discussed sending a Japanese team to Bangladesh to expedite progress on the investment plan.

Bangladesh secured pledges for two yen-loan projects worth a combined 46.56 billion yen, equivalent to approximately US$295.5 million and signed six bilateral cooperation instruments during the visit.

The instruments included a grant agreement of up to 2.12 billion yen (US$13.44 million) for a patrol vessel to strengthen Bangladesh’s coastal security capabilities.

The two countries also signed memorandums of cooperation on improving the business environment, agriculture, the Employment for Skill Development Programme, and fisheries and livestock, alongside a letter of intent on climate change cooperation.

The two loan projects will support improvement of the investment environment in Bangladesh and the second phase of the Upazila Governance and Development Project.

Beyond the government-level agreements, 17 memorandums of understanding (MoUs) were signed between private-sector entities at the Japan External Trade Organization (JETRO), according to State Minister for Foreign Affairs Humaiun Kobir.

On October 28, the prime minister addressed the Bangladesh-Japan Economic Forum Dialogue at JETRO headquarters in Tokyo, inviting Japanese companies to invest in five priority areas: automotive manufacturing, energy, technology and space, high-speed rail and logistics, and agro-processing.

He pledged government support and reforms to improve the business environment.

During the visit, Tarique Rahman also met Japanese political leaders, development partners and business executives, including former prime minister Taro Aso, Japan International Cooperation Agency (JICA) President Dr Akihiko Tanaka, Japan Bank for International Cooperation (JBIC) Governor Kazuhiko Amakawa and JETRO President Susumu Kataoka.

In meetings with representatives of major Japanese companies, including apparel giant Uniqlo, Mitsui & Co., Sumitomo Corporation and JERA, he explored opportunities to expand investment, establish factories, create jobs, facilitate technology transfer and develop skills.

Mechanical fault delays PM’s flight from Japan to Dhaka

The prime minister visited JERA’s liquefied natural gas (LNG) terminal and power plant in Futtsu and the Nittsu Logistics Hub in Ichikawa on October 27 to observe Japan’s energy and logistics facilities.

On Thursday, he travelled to Nagoya and visited Toyota Motor Corporation’s Motomachi factory and the Toyota Commemorative Museum of Industry and Technology, where he observed Japan’s automotive manufacturing capabilities.

The visit comes as Bangladesh and Japan seek to expand economic engagement following the signing of their first-ever Economic Partnership Agreement (EPA) in February 2026, providing a new framework for strengthening trade and commercial ties.

Japan has long been one of Bangladesh’s major development partners, supporting key infrastructure projects, including Dhaka metro rail, the third terminal of Hazrat Shahjalal International Airport and Matarbari deep-sea port.

item.title: Netanyahu, at risk of losing power, steps up attacks on Israel’s Arab parties
item.description:
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu alleged on Thursday, without providing evidence, that Arab parties’ record gains in an election this week were driven in part by voter fraud, a charge rejected by Arab leaders who accused the premier of incitement.

The allegation represents an escalation of rhetoric against Arab parties by Netanyahu and his far-right partners after high Arab turnout in a national ballot on Tuesday effectively blocked a smooth path to power for either him or his main rivals.

Israeli officials said on Thursday that the authorities were probing fraud allegations, though the election’s integrity was not systematically compromised.

Analysts and critics say that by stepping up attacks on Arab parties, Netanyahu may be trying to ensure his main rival, Gadi Eisenkot, feels unable to even consider forming a minority government with Arab help that could oust him from power.

Netanyahu’s goal is “delegitimising any Arab-Jewish cooperation”, said Eytan Gilboa, professor of politics at Reichman University.

Tuesday’s tightly fought election has produced no clear winner and is likely to be followed by weeks of protracted negotiations over a new government.

With nearly 99% of votes counted, Netanyahu’s nationalist-religious bloc held a modest lead in seats over a bloc of right-wing and centre-left parties led by Eisenkot, with both men’s coalitions short of the 61 seats needed for a majority in parliament.

Parties representing Israel’s 21% Arab minority were projected to win an unprecedented 19 seats, leaving Eisenkot’s bloc, which has 48 seats against Netanyahu’s camp of 53, with no path to power without broad Arab backing.

Eisenkot has so far ruled out including the parties in government but his camp could try to form a minority government with Arab support from the outside.

Election Integrity Not Systematically Compromised, Officials Say

Ahmad Tibi, one of the leaders of the Arab Joint List party, said Netanyahu has launched a “toxic campaign” meant to undermine the election results.

“This entire campaign is directed against Eisenkot, to prevent him, intimidate and scare him off forming a government that relies on external support from the Joint List or Ra’am,” Tibi told Reuters.

During and after Tuesday’s election, Netanyahu and his allies warned against rising Arab turnout and his right-wing Likud party issued statements accusing the Arab parties of “stealing the vote.”

It demanded police and the Shin Bet domestic intelligence service investigate incidents of suspected election bribery and intimidation at ballot stations in Arab towns. It said it possessed evidence of such activity but has not presented it to the public.

The police say they have arrested at least seven people since Tuesday in Israel’s south, where many Arabs live, on suspicion of voter fraud.

On Thursday, the head of Israel’s Central Election Committee, Supreme Court jurist Noam Sohlberg, said he had asked the Shin Bet to investigate suspicions that unidentified foreign players had tried to intervene in the election.

Likud seized on Sohlberg’s request, alleging an attack on Israel’s democracy, “an Islamisation of Israel and the toppling of the right-wing in order to bring about IDF withdrawal and defeat on all fronts, foremost Iran.”

Likud said Qatar was behind the alleged election intervention, which Qatar denied.

Ra’am head Mansour Abbas said his party was not involved and urged a full investigation.

“We have one message in response to the campaign of incitement and delegitimization he (Netanyahu) is waging against Arab citizens: Nothing will come of it, because there is nothing there,” Abbas said in a statement.

In a letter sent to a parliamentarian and published by the Central Election Committee, the committee said that there was “no base for claims that there was systematic harm to the election’s integrity.”

Shin Bet said that its investigation was focused only on those involved and should not cast aspersions on “an entire sector that went out to vote democratically and legally.”

Israeli president: ‘we must not tarnish an entire community’

The coalition that last toppled Netanyahu, in 2021, for the first time in Israel’s history relied on an Arab party — Ra’am, which has Islamist roots. But Eisenkot’s camp would need backing from the Arab-dominated Joint List, which includes an explicitly anti-Zionist party.

Eisenkot said in a statement that the investigation into possible election meddling must be carried out without politicians intervening.

“Likud and Netanyahu have set out on an orchestrated organised campaign to delegitimise the election results,” Eisenkot said.

After vote tallying is completed, President Isaac Herzog will consult with party chairs and choose a candidate who he thinks has the best chance to form a government.

On Thursday, he said the allegations must be investigated.

“But even at a moment like this, we must not tarnish an entire community that sought to exercise its right to vote and take an active part in democracy,” Herzog said.

item.title: Lack of planning evident at every level of Bangladesh’s education system
item.description:
Its name is Harvard International College. In reality, it has no functioning academic activities. Finding the college proved difficult. On 8 October, following the address on Shaheed Hariz Road in Jagannathpur, under Dhaka’s Bhatara police station, several local residents were asked about the institution, but none could initially point the way. Eventually, a shopkeeper gestured towards a building. The gate of the dilapidated building bore the name “Rainbow Model High School” on a wall beside it.

There was no one on the ground floor. On the second floor, a man introduced himself as Anwar Hossain, the college’s vice-principal. He said Harvard International College operated there. However, there were no signs of any college activities inside. The place looked more like an ordinary kindergarten or coaching centre.

Asked how many students had enrolled in Class XI this year, the vice-principal said he did not know and that the principal would have the information. The principal could not be found there either.

The education board later confirmed that not a single student had applied for admission to the college’s Class XI programme, even after students were given two rounds of applications this year.

Although students can apply to colleges through a centralised online admission system, not a single applicant included this college on their preference list. Yet, the college remains operational on paper, with 150 seats and teachers on its payroll.

Harvard International College is an example of the widespread mismanagement in the country’s education system. Such a lack of planning is not confined to the college level. From primary to higher education, institutions and seats are being expanded without properly aligning them with student demand, teacher availability, infrastructure and employment opportunities. This has been going on for years.

Some institutions have teachers but no students, while others have students but no teachers. Some universities operate without permanent campuses, while some technical institutions continue to exist despite having no students for years.

Major imbalances and teacher shortages in primary education

The lack of planning begins at the primary level. According to the 2024 Annual Primary School Census, Bangladesh has 118,607 primary schools, both public and private.

Primary education in the country covers pre-primary through Class V. A total of 20.183 million students receive education through 25 types of educational institutions and service providers. Of these, approximately 10.62 million students attend 65,567 government primary schools.

This means that around 45 per cent of all primary schools are privately operated, even though the state is constitutionally responsible for providing free and compulsory primary education.

The government does not have precise figures on the number of kindergartens among private primary schools either. In 2024, the Ministry of Primary and Mass Education estimated that there were around 44,000 nursery schools, kindergartens and privately operated schools. At the time, only about 20 per cent had received academic recognition or registration.

In other words, the government lacks a comprehensive picture of how many kindergartens are operating across the country, where they are located, how many students they teach, how many teachers they employ and which curricula they follow.

Kindergartens generally provide education from playgroup through Class V, although many institutions extend their programmes to Class VIII or even Class X.

Recently, however, State Minister for Primary and Mass Education Bobby Hajjaj said at an event that all private primary schools, kindergartens and English-medium primary institutions would be brought under government supervision alongside government schools. Similar plans had been announced under previous governments as well.

There are more than 65,000 headteacher posts in government primary schools, of which over 36,000 are vacant. Although 12,830 assistant teachers joined this month, around 3,000 posts in that category remain vacant.

Following a ruling by the country's highest court in July, the Ministry of Primary and Mass Education has begun the process of promoting teachers to fill more than 36,000 vacant headteacher posts.

Data from several government and private studies and surveys indicate that students are failing to learn what they are expected to know at their respective ages and grade levels.

In June, the Compulsory Primary Education Implementation Unit inspected 341 schools in Dhaka city, nearly 600 in Dhaka district, 547 in Narayanganj and 611 in Munshiganj.

Its report found that many young students could not correctly pronounce several Bangla letters. They also struggled with conjunct consonants. Their weaknesses in English and mathematics were particularly noticeable.

Chaos in secondary education

The number of educational institutions offering secondary education has risen to 21,314 from 12,012 in 1995.

In addition, around 150 government secondary schools have been offering primary education for years. However, no separate teacher posts have been created for the primary sections. Secondary school teachers are teaching primary-level students despite having no separate training in primary education.

College sections are also operating at 10 government secondary schools, but no separate staffing structures have been established for these additional levels.

Meanwhile, 547 government primary schools offer education up to Class VIII. The teachers at these schools are also primary-level teachers. More than 70,000 students attend these institutions.

Altogether, secondary-level enrolment exceeded 8.638 million in 2025.

Under this poorly planned system, the same teachers are often required to teach students at different educational levels.

According to the recently published Bangladesh Education Statistics 2025 report by the Bangladesh Bureau of Educational Information and Statistics (BANBEIS), 9,982 teachers teaching English at secondary schools did not have English as a subject at the bachelor's degree level. Mathematics shows a similar pattern: 10,169 teachers teaching the subject did not study mathematics at the bachelor's level.

According to the Directorate of Secondary and Higher Education (DSHE), Bangladesh has 702 government secondary schools, with 15,293 approved assistant teacher posts. More than 3,000 of these posts are vacant. Nearly 375 headteacher posts are also vacant.

The situation at Zakiganj Government Girls' High School in Sylhet illustrates the severity of the teacher shortage. The school currently has 486 students but only two teachers. To cope with the situation, several part-time teachers have been hired temporarily.

Another major shortcoming concerns information and communication technology (ICT) education. Although ICT became compulsory at the secondary level in 2013, separate teacher posts for the subject have still not been created in government secondary schools, 13 years later.

As a result, teachers of mathematics, business studies and science are being trained to teach ICT, or are assigned ICT classes as needed.

College seats are increasing, but students are missing

One of the starkest examples of poor planning is this year's Class XI admission process.

Across 11 education boards, 1,829,485 candidates sat for the SSC and equivalent examinations this year. More than 1.144 million passed.

There are 8,180 colleges and madrasas eligible to enrol students in Class XI. Across the country, these institutions offered 2,601,779 seats at that level.

In contrast, only 1,003,288 students were finally selected for admission in the first two rounds, leaving around 1.6 million seats vacant. A total of 416 colleges and madrasas received no applications at all during the first two rounds. The third round of admissions is now under way.

The number of higher secondary colleges, degree-pass colleges, honours colleges and postgraduate colleges has also continued to grow. In 2009, there were 3,347 such institutions. By 2025, the number had risen to 4,936.

However, figures from the past three years show that student enrolment at these colleges has been declining steadily.

Technical institutions expand, but some face closure

Increasing the proportion of students enrolled in technical education is a major government objective. The target is to raise the share of students in technical and vocational education to 30 per cent by 2030.

However, simply increasing the number of institutions and seats has not been enough to achieve this goal.

According to data from the Bangladesh Technical Education Board for the 2024–25 fiscal year, technical education was being offered at 12,932 institutions nationwide, with more than 1.974 million seats.

In contrast, approximately 975,000 students enrolled during that fiscal year, leaving a substantial number of seats vacant.

Some institutions are now being shut down because they have no students.

Recently, the education board suspended admissions at 246 technical institutions after they failed to enrol any students for three consecutive years. Of these, 137 offered diploma-level programmes and 109 offered HSC-BMT programmes in business management and technology.

The authorities have also initiated steps to suspend admissions at another 112 institutions and revoke their approval to conduct classes.

Earlier, 621 institutions offering vocational education were issued show-cause notices for failing to enrol students or conduct academic activities for extended periods.

Madrasa education continues to expand

Madrasa education is another major component of the country's education system. More than 4.25 million students study in madrasas, including those at the ebtedayee primary level.

The number of madrasas offering education beyond the primary level stood at 7,820 in 2002. By 2025, this had increased to 9,296.

According to BANBEIS data, more than 2.84 million students were enrolled last year in madrasas offering Dakhil, Alim, Fazil (pass), Fazil (honours) and Kamil programmes, up from more than 2.796 million the previous year.

In other words, the number of madrasas increased by 27 in a year, while student enrolment rose by more than 43,000.

These figures do not include Qawmi madrasas.

How many more universities are needed?

Bangladesh currently has 61 public universities and 117 approved private universities.

Despite the growing number of universities, the country continues to face problems with the quality of higher education and a shortage of employment opportunities.

A recent report by the International Monetary Fund (IMF) highlighted the high rate of unemployment among educated young people. According to the report, 36 out of every 100 educated young people in Bangladesh are unemployed.

A substantial proportion of young people graduating from the National University also remain outside employment.

Research by the Bangladesh Institute of Development Studies (BIDS) found that approximately 28 per cent of graduates from colleges affiliated with the National University are unemployed.

One reason for the high unemployment rate is that employment opportunities have not expanded at the same pace as the number of universities and graduates. At the same time, links between university education and industry and the workplace remain weak.

Consequently, many students enter the job market without the skills required by employers, despite holding degrees.

Higher education also suffers from inadequate infrastructure planning. As many as 25 public universities still lack their own permanent campuses.

Furthermore, some universities originally established with a particular emphasis on science and technology have introduced subjects such as humanities, social sciences, business studies and even agriculture.

Yet plans to establish more universities continue. Applications have been submitted for approval to establish more than 10 private universities, and the University Grants Commission (UGC) is assessing their feasibility.

There are also plans to establish public universities in Cox's Bazar and several other districts.

A comprehensive approach is needed

Although the problems at different levels of education may appear distinct, they stem from a common underlying crisis: the expansion of institutions without aligning them with educational needs and practical realities. Political influence has also played a role in many cases.

Educationist Manzoor Ahmed, emeritus professor at BRAC University, told Prothom Alo that the current state of poorly planned education had not emerged overnight. Years of allowing this situation to continue have created disorder throughout the education system. Education has never received sufficient priority in political decision-making. Various government initiatives appear fragmented and disconnected.

He recommended setting medium-term goals and strategies for the major subsectors of education and implementing coordinated programmes to achieve them.

“Instead of addressing the problems at one level in isolation, we must take a comprehensive view of the entire system,” he said.
